kamelets.name: avro-deserialize-action
kamelets.title: Avro Deserialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message of Avro binary data back into a JSON object, using the Avro schema the data was written with.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message of Avro binary data back into a JSON object, using the Avro schema the data was written with.

Use it to read records that arrive in Avro, a compact binary format described by a schema, for example from a Kafka topic, and work on them as JSON. To turn JSON into Avro, use `avro-serialize-action`; for Protobuf, use `protobuf-deserialize-action`.

Input: Avro binary data, as bytes, without the schema in it, such as `avro-serialize-action` writes.

Output: the body is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`) with one field for each field of the schema. The `Content-Type` header is removed. Put `json-serialize-action` after this action to get JSON text.

Good to know: Avro data does not say which schema it was written with, so the schema must be the one the writer used. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: avro-serialize-action
kamelets.title: Avro Serialize Action
kamelets.summary: Turns each message, a JSON object, into Avro binary data that follows the Avro schema you give.
kamelets.description:
Turns each message, a JSON object, into Avro binary data that follows the Avro schema you give.

Use it to send records in Avro, a compact binary format described by a schema, to a system that expects it, such as a Kafka topic whose readers decode Avro. To turn Avro back into JSON, use `avro-deserialize-action`; for Protobuf, use `protobuf-serialize-action`.

Input: parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`) whose fields match the schema. JSON text fails: put `json-deserialize-action` before this action to parse it.

Output: the body is the Avro binary data, as bytes, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/avro`.

Good to know: the schema is not written into the data, so whoever reads it needs the same schema. A message fails when it lacks a field of the schema, has a field the schema does not know, or has a value of the wrong type. When `schema` is not set, the schema found by an earlier `resolve-pojo-schema-action` is used.

kamelets.name: azure-cosmosdb-sink
kamelets.title: Azure CosmosDB Sink
kamelets.summary: Creates an item (a JSON document) in a container of Azure Cosmos DB for each message, from the JSON object in the body.
kamelets.description:
Creates an item (a JSON document) in a container of Azure Cosmos DB for each message, from the JSON object in the body.

Use it to store orders, events or profiles as JSON documents in Cosmos DB. To receive the changes made to a container, use `azure-cosmosdb-source`.

Input: the body is one item as JSON text: a JSON object with an `id` field, such as `{"id": "1001", "region": "EU"}`. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The partition key value of the item comes from the `itemPartitionKey` option or, when the option is not set, from the `itemPartitionKey` header (or `ce-itemPartitionKey`) of each message.

Output: the body afterwards is the item as it was created, as a Map, with the fields that Cosmos DB adds.

Good to know: a message without a partition key value fails, and so does an item whose `id` already exists in the same partition: the sink creates items and never replaces them.

kamelets.name: azure-cosmosdb-source
kamelets.title: Azure CosmosDB Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the items created or changed in a container of Azure Cosmos DB, through its change feed, as a JSON array per batch.
kamelets.description:
Receives the items created or changed in a container of Azure Cosmos DB, through its change feed, as a JSON array per batch.

Use it to react to new or updated documents, for example to copy them to a search index, a cache or Kafka. To create items, use `azure-cosmosdb-sink`.

Output: the body is a JSON array of the items of one batch, as bytes, each item with the fields that Cosmos DB adds, such as `_etag`.

Good to know: it reads only the changes made after it first starts, and it does not see deleted items. It keeps its position in a lease container, `camel-lease` in the database `databaseName` unless set otherwise, which must exist unless `createLeaseContainerIfNotExists` is true.

kamelets.name: azure-eventhubs-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Eventhubs Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an event to an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, the Azure service for event streams.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an event to an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, the Azure service for event streams.

Use it to publish events, such as clicks, sensor readings or changes, for stream processing or for other applications to read. To receive them, use `azure-eventhubs-source`.

Input: the body becomes the body of the event: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. A List is sent as one event per element. The optional `partition-id` header (or `ce-partition-id`) is the partition to send to, such as `0`; without it, Event Hubs chooses one.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the shared access policy needs the Send right.

kamelets.name: azure-eventhubs-source
kamelets.title: Azure Eventhubs Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the events of an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, one message per event, and saves how far it has read in an Azure Storage blob container.
kamelets.description:
Receives the events of an event hub in Azure Event Hubs, one message per event, and saves how far it has read in an Azure Storage blob container.

Use it to process event streams, such as telemetry or changes, that other applications send to Event Hubs. To send events, use `azure-eventhubs-sink`.

Output: the body is the body of the event, as bytes. The headers give its partition (`CamelAzureEventHubsPartitionId`), offset, sequence number and the time it was enqueued, and `CamelAzureEventHubsMetadata` holds the custom properties of the event.

Good to know: when no position has been saved yet, it starts with the events that arrive after it starts, not the older ones. It reads as the `$Default` consumer group. It saves its position (a checkpoint) in `blobContainerName` every 500 events or every 5 seconds, so after a restart some events can be read again.

kamelets.name: azure-functions-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Function Sink
kamelets.summary: Calls a function in Azure Functions over HTTP for each message, with the message as the body of the request.
kamelets.description:
Calls a function in Azure Functions over HTTP for each message, with the message as the body of the request.

Use it to run your own serverless code on each message, such as an enrichment, a notification or a calculation. For any other web service, use `http-sink`.

Input: the body is sent as the request body, as text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `Content-Type` header is sent as the content type of the request, and the other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as HTTP headers.

Output: when it is used inside a route, the body afterwards is the response of the function, and the `CamelHttpResponseCode` header its status code.

Good to know: a response with a status code outside 200 to 299 fails the message. The `key` is sent as the `code` query parameter of the request.

kamelets.name: azure-servicebus-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Servicebus Sink
kamelets.summary: Sends each message to a queue or a topic in Azure Service Bus, the Azure message broker.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message to a queue or a topic in Azure Service Bus, the Azure message broker.

Use it to hand work or events to other applications through Service Bus, such as orders to process, or notifications for all the subscribers of a topic. For simple storage queues, use `azure-storage-queue-sink`.

Input: the body is sent as text: text, bytes or a stream are read as text. A Map is sent as its text form, so turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. A List is sent as one message per element. The optional `CamelAzureServiceBusApplicationProperties` header, a Map, sets the custom properties of the message.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: the shared access policy of the connection string needs the Send right.

kamelets.name: azure-servicebus-source
kamelets.title: Azure Servicebus Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the messages of a queue, or of a topic subscription, in Azure Service Bus, one message each.
kamelets.description:
Receives the messages of a queue, or of a topic subscription, in Azure Service Bus, one message each.

Use it to process work or events that other applications send through Service Bus. To read new blobs from Event Grid events that arrive in a Service Bus queue, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the body of the Service Bus message, as bytes. The headers give its ID (`CamelAzureServiceBusMessageId`), its custom properties (`CamelAzureServiceBusApplicationProperties`, a Map), its content type, correlation ID, subject, enqueued time and delivery count.

Good to know: with the default `serviceBusReceiveMode` of `PEEK_LOCK`, a message is removed only once it has been processed; a message whose processing fails is given back and received again, until Service Bus moves it to the dead-letter queue after the maximum delivery count (10 by default). With `RECEIVE_AND_DELETE`, a message is removed as soon as it is received, so a failure loses it. For a topic, set `serviceBusType` to `topic` and `subscriptionName`.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-append-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Append Sink
kamelets.summary: Adds each message at the end of an append blob in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header, and creates the blob when it does not exist yet.
kamelets.description:
Adds each message at the end of an append blob in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header, and creates the blob when it does not exist yet.

Use it to collect log lines, audit records or CSV rows from many messages into one growing blob. To write each message as a blob of its own, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the data to add: text, bytes or a stream. It is added as it is, so end each line with a line break yourself. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the blob, such as `logs/app.log`. Without it, each message goes to a new blob with a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageBlobAppendOffset` and `CamelAzureStorageBlobCommittedBlockCount` describe the append.

Good to know: the container must exist: a missing container fails the message. A name that is already used by a block blob, such as one written by `azure-storage-blob-sink`, fails the message too.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-changefeed-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Changefeed Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the change feed of an Azure Storage account at a fixed interval, one message per event, such as a blob that was created or deleted.
kamelets.description:
Reads the change feed of an Azure Storage account at a fixed interval, one message per event, such as a blob that was created or deleted.

Use it to audit or replicate the changes made to the blobs of a whole storage account. To read the blobs themselves, use `azure-storage-blob-source`; to react to new blobs as they arrive, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the `data` part of the event, as JSON text. The headers `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-eventType`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-subject` (the path of the blob), `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-eventTime`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-id`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-topic`, `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-dataVersion` and `azure-storage-blob-changefeed-metadataVersion` give the rest of the event.

Good to know: the change feed must be turned on for the storage account (in the Azure portal: the storage account, then Data protection, then Enable blob change feed); otherwise every poll fails. It does not remember what it has read: every poll returns the whole change feed again, so the same events come again on every poll.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-event-based-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Event-based Source
kamelets.summary: Receives the Event Grid events of an Azure Storage account from a Service Bus queue and can read the content of each new blob in a container.
kamelets.description:
Receives the Event Grid events of an Azure Storage account from a Service Bus queue and can read the content of each new blob in a container.

Use it to react quickly to new blobs, such as uploaded files, without reading the container over and over. It needs an Event Grid subscription on the storage account that sends the events, in the Event Grid schema, to a Service Bus queue. To read the container on a timer instead, use `azure-storage-blob-source`.

Output: when `getBlob` is false, the default, the body is the Event Grid event as JSON (an Azure `BinaryData`, which converts to text or bytes). When `getBlob` is true, the body of a `Microsoft.Storage.BlobCreated` event for a blob of `containerName` is the content of that blob, as a stream of bytes; the other events are passed on as parsed JSON (a Jackson JSON node).

Good to know: with the default `serviceBusReceiveMode` of `RECEIVE_AND_DELETE`, an event is removed from the queue as soon as it is received, so an event whose processing fails is lost. With `getBlob`, only blobs at the top of the container can be read: an event for a blob in a virtual folder, such as `in/a.txt`, fails. It reads from a queue, not from a topic.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file (a block blob) to a container in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file (a block blob) to a container in Azure Blob Storage, named after the `file` header.

Use it to store documents, exports or event payloads in Azure, for other applications or for archiving. To add each message at the end of one growing blob, such as a log, use `azure-storage-blob-append-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the blob: text, bytes or a stream. Turn structured data such as a Map into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the blob, such as `reports/2026-05.csv`; a `/` in it puts the blob in a virtual folder. Without it, the blob gets a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`, and headers such as `CamelAzureStorageBlobETag` and `CamelAzureStorageBlobLastModified` describe the uploaded blob.

Good to know: a blob with the same name is replaced. The container must exist: a missing container fails the message. The name comes only from `file` or `ce-file`: to copy blobs from `azure-storage-blob-source` and keep their names, set `file` from its `CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName` header first.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-blob-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files (blobs) in a container of Azure Blob Storage, one message per blob, and can delete each blob once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files (blobs) in a container of Azure Blob Storage, one message per blob, and can delete each blob once it has been read.

Use it to process files that another system drops into a container, such as uploaded documents, exported reports or log files. To react to new blobs through Event Grid events instead of reading the container over and over, use `azure-storage-blob-event-based-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the blob, as a stream of bytes. The headers give the name of the blob (`CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName`, with its folder path), its type, content type, size, ETag and last-modified time.

Good to know: blobs are kept after they are read, so the same blobs are read again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default; set `deleteAfterRead` to true to delete each blob once it has been processed. It reads all the blobs of the container, those in virtual folders too. With `deleteAfterRead`, the blob deleted is the one named in the `CamelAzureStorageBlobBlobName` header when processing ends, so do not change that header.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-datalake-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Data Lake Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a file system in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a file system in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, named after the `file` header.

Use it to land data for analytics, such as exports, events or reports, in a data lake. For plain blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the file, such as `sales-2026-05.csv`. Without it, the file gets a generated unique name.

Output: the body afterwards is `true`.

Good to know: by default it logs in as an app registration, with `clientId`, `clientSecret` and `tenantId`, so that app needs a role on the account that allows writing, such as Storage Blob Data Contributor.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-datalake-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Blob Data Lake Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a file system of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, one message per file, on every poll.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a file system of Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, one message per file, on every poll.

Use it to process files that land in a data lake, such as exports or reports. For plain blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-source`, which can also delete what it reads.

Output: the body is the content of the file, as a stream of bytes. The `CamelAzureStorageDataLakeFileName` header is the name of the file, and other headers give its size, content type, ETag and last-modified time.

Good to know: it neither deletes nor moves the files, so it reads all of them again on every poll, every 500 milliseconds by default. It reads the files at the top of the file system: files in directories are not read.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-files-sink
kamelets.title: Azure Storage Files Sink
kamelets.summary: Uploads each message as a file to a directory of a file share in Azure Files, named after the `file` header.
kamelets.description:
Uploads each message as a file to a directory of a file share in Azure Files, named after the `file` header.

Use it to drop files where applications or people that mount the share can read them, such as reports or exports. For blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-sink`.

Input: the body is the content of the file: text, bytes or a stream. A Map fails: turn it into JSON text first, for example with `json-serialize-action`. The optional `file` header (or `ce-file`) is the name of the file; only its last part is used, so `reports/2026/data.csv` is written as `data.csv` in `directoryName`. Without it, the file gets a generated unique name.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: a file with the same name is replaced. Missing directories are created.

kamelets.name: azure-storage-files-source
kamelets.title: Azure Storage File Source
kamelets.summary: Reads the files in a directory of a file share in Azure Files, one message per file, and can delete each file once it has been read.
kamelets.description:
Reads the files in a directory of a file share in Azure Files, one message per file, and can delete each file once it has been read.

Use it to process files that people or applications put on a share, such as scanned documents or exports. For blob containers, use `azure-storage-blob-source`.

Output: the body is the content of the file, which converts to text, bytes or a stream. The `CamelFileName` header is the path of the file from `directoryName`, `CamelFileNameOnly` its name, and `CamelFileLength` and `CamelFileLastModified` its size and last-modified time.

kamelets.summary: Converts the body of each message into the data type you name, such as plain text, bytes, JSON, Avro or Protobuf, and sets the `Content-Type` header to match.
kamelets.description:
Converts the body of each message into the data type you name, such as plain text, bytes, JSON, Avro or Protobuf, and sets the `Content-Type` header to match.

kamelets.name: dns-dig-action
kamelets.title: DNS DIG Action
kamelets.summary: Asks the DNS for the records of one kind, such as A or MX, of a name, and gives the answer as text, in the format of the `dig` tool.
kamelets.description:
Asks the DNS for the records of one kind, such as A or MX, of a name, and gives the answer as text, in the format of the `dig` tool.

Use it to see the records of a domain, such as its mail (MX) records, for example to check a DNS change. To get only the IP address of a name, use `dns-ip-action`, and to get its address records as JSON, use `dns-lookup-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain-name` header, else from the `ce-domainname` header, else from the body as text. The kind of record comes from the `dns-type` header, else from the `ce-dnstype` header, else it is `A` (the IPv4 addresses).

Output: the body is the whole answer as text, as the `dig` command shows it: the question, the records found, and the status, such as `NOERROR`.

Good to know: a name the DNS does not know does not fail the message: the answer has the status `NXDOMAIN` and no records. The Kamelet has no options; it asks the DNS servers of the machine it runs on.

kamelets.name: dns-ip-action
kamelets.title: DNS IP Action
kamelets.summary: Finds the IP address of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives it as text.
kamelets.description:
Finds the IP address of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives it as text.

Use it to turn a host name into an address for a later step, or to check that a name can be resolved. To see all the address records of a name with how long they may be cached, use `dns-lookup-action`, and to ask for other kinds of record, such as mail (MX) records, use `dns-dig-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain` header, else from the `ce-domain` header, else from the body as text.

Output: the body is one IP address, as text, such as `151.101.2.132`.

Good to know: when a name has several addresses, only one of them is given. A name the DNS does not know fails the message with an unknown host error. The headers are `domain` and `ce-domain`, not `domain-name` as for `dns-lookup-action` and `dns-dig-action`. The Kamelet has no options; it uses the name resolution of the machine it runs on.

kamelets.name: dns-lookup-action
kamelets.title: DNS Lookup Action
kamelets.summary: Asks the DNS for the address records of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives them as JSON.
kamelets.description:
Asks the DNS for the address records of a host name, such as `apache.org`, and gives them as JSON.

Use it to check that a name exists in the DNS, or to see its records and how long they may be cached, for example to monitor a domain. To get the IP address of a name, use `dns-ip-action` instead, and to ask for other kinds of record, such as mail (MX) records, use `dns-dig-action`.

Input: the name to look up, taken from the `domain-name` header, else from the `ce-domainname` header, else from the body as text.

Output: the body is a JSON array with one entry per record found. Each entry has the type, the class and the time to live of the record.

Good to know: a name the DNS does not know fails the message with "host not found". The Kamelet has no options; it asks the DNS servers of the machine it runs on.

Before the conversion, the value of the `documentIdHeader` header is captured into the

kamelets.name: drop-field-action
kamelets.title: Drop Field Action
kamelets.summary: Removes one field, chosen by its name, from each message that is a JSON object.
kamelets.description:
Removes one field, chosen by its name, from each message that is a JSON object.

Use it to take out a field that the next system does not accept or should not see, such as an internal ID or a password. To remove several fields, or to keep only some, use `replace-field-action`; to keep the field but hide its value, use `mask-field-action`.

Input: a JSON object, as JSON text or as parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`). Only the fields at the top level of the object are looked at. A JSON array is passed on unchanged; a body that is not JSON fails.

Output: the same object without the field. When the `Content-Type` header is `application/json`, the body is JSON text again; otherwise it is parsed JSON (a Jackson `JsonNode`), which `json-serialize-action` turns into JSON text.

Good to know: a message without the field is passed on unchanged. A field of the same name inside a nested object is not removed.

kamelets.name: drop-header-action
kamelets.title: Drop Header Action
kamelets.summary: Removes one header, given by its name, from each message.
kamelets.description:
Removes one header, given by its name, from each message.

Use it to remove a header that the next step must not see, for example an `Authorization` header with a secret, or a header that would change what a sink does. To remove several headers at once by a pattern, such as all the headers whose names start with `Camel`, use `drop-headers-action`.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body, and the same headers without the one named by `name`. A message without that header passes on unchanged.

Good to know: the name is not case-sensitive: `FOO` also removes the header `foo`.

kamelets.name: drop-headers-action
kamelets.title: Drop Headers Action
kamelets.summary: Removes from each message all the headers whose names match a pattern, such as `Camel*`.
kamelets.description:
Removes from each message all the headers whose names match a pattern, such as `Camel*`.

Use it to remove the internal `Camel*` headers that came with a message from outside before it reaches a sink, or to clear many headers at once before a message goes to another system. To remove a single header by its name, `drop-header-action` is enough.

Input: any message.

Output: the same body, without the headers that match `pattern`. The headers that match `excludePattern` are kept.

Good to know: a pattern is compared with each header name first as an exact name, then as a wildcard when it ends with `*` (`x-*` matches every name that starts with `x-`), and then as a Java regular expression, such as `x-(one|two)`. None of these comparisons is case-sensitive.

Input: a batch from `kafka-batch-source`, or from one of the `kafka-batch-*-registry-*` sources, with `allowManualCommit` set to true and `autoCommitEnable` set to false. It uses the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header of the message, or else that of the last entry of the list.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: without the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header, for example when `allowManualCommit` is false, it does nothing and does not fail.

kamelets.name: kafka-batch-source
kamelets.title: Kafka Batch Source
kamelets.summary: Receives records from one or more topics in Apache Kafka in batches, as one message that holds a list of up to `batchSize` records.
kamelets.description:
Receives records from one or more topics in Apache Kafka in batches, as one message that holds a list of up to `batchSize` records.

Use it to handle many records at once, for example to write them to a database in one go, or to save the position in Kafka only once a whole batch was handled. To handle one record at a time use `kafka-source`.

Output: the body is a List with one entry per record, up to `batchSize`. Each entry is a message of its own, with the value of the record as its body (text), and the key, offset and timestamp of the record in its `CamelKafkaKey`, `CamelKafkaOffset` and `CamelKafkaTimestamp` headers. The record headers are in the entries too, as bytes. The message itself has the `CamelKafkaTopic` and `CamelKafkaPartition` headers. The `kafka-topic`, `kafka-key` and other headers of `kafka-source` are not set.

Good to know: with the default `saslAuthType` of `NONE`, it connects with no login and no TLS. To save the position in Kafka only once a batch was handled, set `allowManualCommit` to true and `autoCommitEnable` to false, and end the flow with `kafka-batch-manual-commit-action`. A new consumer group starts at the newest records, unless `autoOffsetReset` is `earliest`. Without `consumerGroup`, every start uses a new group, so the records sent while the integration was stopped are skipped.

kamelets.name: kafka-manual-commit-action
kamelets.title: Kafka Manual Commit Action
kamelets.summary: Saves in Kafka the position (offset) of the record that `kafka-source` received, so that the record is not received again after a restart.
kamelets.description:
Saves in Kafka the position (offset) of the record that `kafka-source` received, so that the record is not received again after a restart.

Use it to count a record as read only once it was handled, for example once it was written to a database: put it at the end of a flow that starts with `kafka-source`. The records after the last saved position are read again after a restart. For `kafka-batch-source` use `kafka-batch-manual-commit-action`.

Input: any message from `kafka-source` with `allowManualCommit` set to true and `autoCommitEnable` set to false. It uses the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header that the source then sets.

Output: the message is unchanged.

Good to know: without the `CamelKafkaManualCommit` header, for example when `allowManualCommit` is false, it does nothing and does not fail. Saving the position of a record also counts the earlier records of its partition as read.

kamelets.description:
Receives each record written with a JSON Schema from topics in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry secured with Keycloak.

They are also set as `ce-kafkatopic`, `ce-kafkakey` and so on, and as the `CamelKafka*` headers that the Kafka actions read. The record headers become message headers, as text unless `deserializeHeaders` is false.

Without `consumerGroup`, every start uses a new group, so the records sent while the integration was stopped are skipped.

kamelets.name: kafka-not-secured-apicurio-registry-sink

kamelets.summary: Sends each message as an Avro record to a topic in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry secured with Keycloak.
kamelets.description:
Sends each message as an Avro record to a topic in Apache Kafka, with the schema kept in an Apicurio Registry secured with Keycloak.

Use it to publish records that other applications read with the schema of the registry, when the registry needs a Keycloak login and Kafka needs none. When the registry needs no login use `kafka-apicurio-registry-not-secured-sink`; for records without a schema use `kafka-sink`.

Input: the body must be an Avro object, such as an Avro `GenericRecord` or an object of a class generated from the schema; it is written as Avro binary. A body of text is written as an Avro string, and so fails unless the schema is a string. The optional `key` header (or `ce-key`) becomes the key of the record, and the optional `partition-key` header (or `ce-partitionkey`) is the number of the partition to write to. The other headers of the message, except the Camel ones, are sent as record headers.

Kafka is not secured: it connects to the brokers with no login and no TLS.

kamelets.name: langchain4j-ingest-file-source
kamelets.title: LangChain4j Ingest File Source
kamelets.summary: Watch a directory as the source of an ingestion pipeline, with the defaults a knowledge base needs.
kamelets.description:
Watch a directory as the source of an ingestion pipeline, with the defaults a knowledge
base needs.

The defaults: documents are left in place (noop), unchanged files are remembered in a
duplicate register keyed on path, modification time and size, a file still being copied
in is waited for (readLock=changed), and the file name is exposed as the document id in
the CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId header.

Mind the two dedup layers when composing: this source re-delivers an edited file (its
register key changes with the modification time), but a langchain4j-ingest-sink with an
idempotentRepository is first-write-wins by document id - the re-delivered edit would
be skipped. Use a version-aware id, or no sink repository, when documents change.

kamelets.name: langchain4j-ingest-sink
kamelets.title: LangChain4j Ingest Sink
kamelets.summary: Ingest documents into a LangChain4j EmbeddingStore.
kamelets.description:
Ingest documents into a LangChain4j EmbeddingStore.

The payload is split into overlapping segments, embedded in batches and written to the
store, each segment stamped with the pipeline name and the document id.

The document id is read from the `CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId` exchange property
when a prior step captured it (the parser actions do, before the parse), else from the
header named by `documentIdHeader` - the property always wins, so a parsed document
cannot forge its own identity. Bean references are `#bean:name` values; when
`embeddingStore` or `embeddingModel` is not set, the single registry bean of that type is
used. With `idempotentRepository` set, the first write per document id wins - a
re-delivered edited document is skipped, so streams that carry updates need a
version-aware id. The filter options (`includeId`, `excludeId`, `minDocumentSize`,
`documentFilter`) answer rejected deliveries with a filtered outcome that never keeps
a dedup claim.

With `modality` set to `media` the payload (audio, an image, video or a PDF) is embedded
whole, as one vector; the source must deliver raw bytes. A file source re-polls any
document that fails the exchange on every run, so restrict the ids with `includeId` or
the source's `include`.

kamelets.summary: Replaces the values of the fields you name in each message that is a JSON object with a fixed value, such as `XXXX`.

Input: parsed JSON (a Map or a Jackson `JsonNode`) whose fields match the schema. Put `json-deserialize-action` before this action when the body is JSON text.

Output: the body is the Protobuf binary data, as bytes, and the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/protobuf`.

Good to know: JSON text is not turned into Protobuf: it is passed on as it is, yet the `Content-Type` header is set to `application/protobuf`. A message fails when it has a field the schema does not know or a value of the wrong type; a field of the schema that the message lacks is left out, even when it is marked `required`. kamelets.summary: Extract plain text from PDF, office and similar documents in-process with Apache Tika.
kamelets.description:
Extract plain text from PDF, office and similar documents in-process with Apache Tika.

Before the parse, the value of the `documentIdHeader` header is captured into the
`CamelLangChain4jIngestDocumentId` exchange property - Tika copies document metadata
over the headers, so a crafted document could otherwise forge its own identity in steps
that read it later (the langchain4j-ingest sink does). The extracted text is decoded at
a pinned UTF-8 (a document-injected charset header is swept before the conversion), and
after the parse all non-Camel headers are removed: past this action, parsed document
metadata is indistinguishable from caller headers, so it must not travel further. Each
format needs its Tika parser module on the classpath; camel-tika ships the HTML and
text modules, PDF needs org.apache.tika:tika-parser-pdf-module. With `maxDocumentSize`
set, a payload larger than that many bytes fails the exchange before the parse.

For a calendar schedule such as "every weekday at 9:00" use `cron-source` instead, and for a message that counts up use `counter-source`.

Use it to spread the records over one topic per day or per month, in a flow from `kafka-source` to `kafka-sink`, for example to keep or delete them by period. To take the date from a field of a JSON body instead use `message-timestamp-router-action`.

kamelets.summary: Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with an XSLT stylesheet that decides what the result looks like.
kamelets.description:
Converts each message from XML to JSON, or from JSON to XML, with an XSLT stylesheet that decides what the result looks like.

Use it to map the XML of one system to the JSON of another, or the other way round, when the fixed mapping of `xj-identity-action` does not give the shape you need.
